newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria impoverished by delayed reforms, big debt.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria impoverished by delayed reforms, big debt.

text.p: Bulgaria's failure to speed up reforms has sparked a huge build-up of state loss-makers' debts and further impoverishment, the National Statistics Institute (NSI) said on Thursday.

"We have seen a continual impoverishement of the nation in the past several years of transition to a market economy. The slump this year is graver than ever," NSI expert Bogdan Bogdanov told a news conference.
"Possiblities for creating a strong middle class are declining," Bogdanov added.
The real value of the average income of 6,000 interviewed households fell 51 percent in July this year versus a year ago.
Hikes on prices of electricity, heating and other utilities have made them unaffordable for many Bulgarians. People on state wages and pensioners said they may not survive the winter.
The NSI saw Bulgaria's business climate also deteriorate.
"Private and state firms were plagued (by) rising raw material prices, insolvency, fiancial problems and unceratian economic conditions," said NSI epxert Dimiter Fratev.

Debts of state-owned lossmakers jumped more than 40 percent to more than 616 billion levs this June from the previous year. These debts were accumulated by 2,883 enterprises or 49.5 percent of all state-owned firms.

The Socialist government has delayed closing down some 64 loss making state enterprises, agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) two months ago. The IMF postponed a $115 million loan until these loss-makers were shut-down.

Unpaid interest to banks amounted to 42 billion levs this June, which is a 165-percent rise on June 1995. NSI attributed the failure to pay these dues to high interest rates, which were at a record-high 108 percent five months ago in a bid to support the lev and curb inflation.
Dues to suppliers were 109 bilion levs, or a 161.4-percent rise on June 1995.
These enterprises owed their employees a total of 21.1 billion levs of unpaid wages this June, which is a 152-percent increase on last June.
